    15  /-!
    16  # Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
    17  
    18  We prove various versions of the
    19  [fundamental theorem of calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_calculus)
    20  for interval integrals in `ℝ`.
    21  
    22  Recall that its first version states that the function `(u, v) ↦ ∫ x in u..v, f x` has derivative
    23  `(δu, δv) ↦ δv • f b - δu • f a` at `(a, b)` provided that `f` is continuous at `a` and `b`,
    24  and its second version states that, if `f` has an integrable derivative on `[a, b]`, then
    25  `∫ x in a..b, f' x = f b - f a`.
    26  
    27  ## Main statements
    28  
    29  ### FTC-1 for Lebesgue measure
    30  
    31  We prove several versions of FTC-1, all in the `intervalIntegral` namespace. Many of them follow
    32  the naming scheme `integral_has(Strict?)(F?)Deriv(Within?)At(_of_tendsto_ae?)(_right|_left?)`.
    33  They formulate FTC in terms of `Has(Strict?)(F?)Deriv(Within?)At`.
    34  Let us explain the meaning of each part of the name:
    35  
    36  * `Strict` means that the theorem is about strict differentiability, see `HasStrictDerivAt` and
    37    `HasStrictFDerivAt`;
    38  * `F` means that the theorem is about differentiability in both endpoints; incompatible with
    39    `_right|_left`;
    40  * `Within` means that the theorem is about one-sided derivatives, see below for details;
    41  * `_of_tendsto_ae` means that instead of continuity the theorem assumes that `f` has a finite limit
    42    almost surely as `x` tends to `a` and/or `b`;
    43  * `_right` or `_left` mean that the theorem is about differentiability in the right (resp., left)
    44    endpoint.
    45  
    46  We also reformulate these theorems in terms of `(f?)deriv(Within?)`. These theorems are named
    47  `(f?)deriv(Within?)_integral(_of_tendsto_ae?)(_right|_left?)` with the same meaning of parts of the
    48  name.
    49  
    50  ### One-sided derivatives
"}]
